blocks.text: This chapter presents prophetic authority as contested, not self-authenticating. Jeremiah’s enacted yoke and his warning to submit to Babylon directly oppose other prophetic assurances that submission will not be necessary and that the temple vessels will soon return. A disputed interpretive reading sees this conflict developed especially in the later confrontation with Hananiah, where claims about yokes, peace, timing, and outcomes are tested against one another.

The received book of Jeremiah combines poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, repeated accounts, restoration collections, oracles concerning nations, and an appendix. One practical outline places chapters 26–29 together within the book, while recognizing that the book’s long compositional and textual history remains debated.
